statement: In two small field studies of young adults who took ecstasy tablets of unknown content at a weekend, the day after was marked by tiredness and short sleep, while mood was no lower than in the comparison groups. In London (Curran and Travill, 1997), 12 people who said they had taken ecstasy at a club rated themselves the next day as more lacking in energy and more physically tired than 12 people recovering from a night of heavy drinking (on 0-100 scales, 82 against 66 and 79 against 65), and made fewer correct subtractions in two minutes (14 against 27; they were lower on every test day, including mid-week; the authors could not say whether this was a direct drug effect or whether lack of sleep also contributed), while their depression questionnaire scores were the same as the drinking group's (8.7 against 8.3). In Melbourne (Scott et al., 2013), 34 people who took ecstasy slept about two hours less that night than 21 people who also use ecstasy but abstained that week (5.9 against 8.1 hours), yet the next day, against each person's own baseline a week earlier, the two groups did not differ in distress, mood ratings or clinician-rated depression, anxiety and hostility. Neither study tested the tablets or measured sleep objectively, people chose what they took, in London the assessor knew who had taken what, and there was no measurement before the drug night, with next-day tests at home in the afternoon rather than in the club at night. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Two small studies followed young people around a weekend. The day after taking ecstasy, people felt much more tired and low on energy, and had slept about two hours less, than people who had not taken it. Their mood that day was no worse than that of people recovering from heavy drinking, or of people who also use ecstasy but skipped it that weekend. Nobody tested the pills or measured sleep with a machine.
population: Young adults who use ecstasy, recruited at one London club (aged 20 to 27) or through advertisements in Melbourne (aged 18 to 35), studied around a weekend of use
exposure: Ecstasy tablets taken at a weekend, by self-report; contents not tested (amounts are study conditions in the study cards)
comparator: People who drank alcohol but took no illicit drug that night (London); people who use ecstasy but chose not to that weekend, each compared with their own baseline (Melbourne)
outcome: Next-day tiredness and energy, hours of sleep, depression and mood ratings, clinician-rated symptoms, a subtraction test
magnitude: London, day 2 (0-100 mm scales): lack of energy 82.2 (SD 11.4) against 65.8 (8.5) and physical tiredness 78.9 (11.7) against 64.5 (5.9), group x day p<0.001 for both; correct subtractions 14.2 (6.7) against 26.6 (10.7), group p<0.01; Beck Depression Inventory 8.7 (3.8) against 8.3 (5.2). Melbourne: sleep 5.85 h (2.14) against 8.06 h (1.93), p<0.001; no group or group x time effect on Kessler-10 distress or 1-10 mood; clinician-rated change scores p>0.05.

evidence.locator: Table 3, lack of energy and physical tiredness rows (p. 828); Results, Bodily Symptoms Scale paragraph (p. 826, left column)
evidence.extracted: Day 2 ratings on visual analogue scales, ecstasy against alcohol group: lack of energy 82.2 (SD 11.4) against 65.8 (8.5), up from 10.6 and 38.8 on the night; physical tiredness 78.9 (11.7) against 64.5 (5.9); group x day p<0.001 for both. The text says the ecstasy group went from high energy on day 1 to marked lack of energy and tiredness on day 2, persisting somewhat to day 5.

evidence.locator: Table 1, serial sevens row (p. 824); Results, Serial sevens paragraph (pp. 824-825); Table 2, BDI row (p. 827)
evidence.extracted: Correct subtractions in two minutes on day 2: 14.2 (SD 6.7) in the ecstasy group against 26.6 (10.7) in the alcohol group; the ecstasy group made fewer at every testing point (day 5: 25.1 against 31.1), group p<0.01 and group x day p<0.05, most marked on day 2; errors did not differ. Beck Depression Inventory on day 2: 8.7 (3.8) against 8.3 (5.2).
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/MDMA/Curran_1997_WeekendHighMidweekLow..pdf (published version, scanned copy; Tables 1 and 2 read on rendered page images)

evidence.locator: Table 5, hours of sleep row (p. 58); Results, Group comparisons: mood, K10 and Subjective mood paragraphs (p. 57, right column); BPRS clinician ratings (p. 58, left column)
evidence.extracted: Hours of sleep the night before Day 1: 5.85 (SD 2.14) in the 34 who took ecstasy against 8.06 (1.93) in the 21 abstainers, p<0.001. K10 distress: no main effect of group and no group x time interaction. Subjective mood: no group or group x day effect; both groups lower than baseline at Day 1 (F(1,52) = 4.60, p = 0.04). BPRS depression, anxiety and hostility change scores did not differ between groups (p > 0.05).

evidence.locator: Method, Procedure (p. 823, right column); Discussion, paragraph continuing from p. 829 (p. 830, left column)
evidence.extracted: Most of the ecstasy group reported lack of sleep on day 2, and the authors cannot say whether the day-2 subtraction deficit was a direct drug effect or whether lack of sleep also contributed; sleep was not measured. Day 1 was tested in the club at night and day 2 at home between 12:00 and 16:00, so time and place changed with the day; there was no measurement before the drug night.

risk_of_bias.note: Both observational: self-chosen exposure, untested tablets, self-reported outcomes; the London study has no pre-drug measurement and an unblinded assessor (ROBINS-E very high), the Melbourne study a baseline but self-selected groups (high).

inconsistency.note: Both studies agree that next-day mood did not differ from the comparison group and that the night cost sleep or energy.

indirectness.note: Worded for real-world weekend use in the samples studied.

imprecision.note: 12 and 12, 35 and 21 people; no intervals; a small next-day mood difference cannot be excluded.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low. Status replicated: two independent field studies, in London and Melbourne with different comparison groups, both found tiredness or lost sleep and no lower mood than the comparison group the next day. The worse subtraction scores in London cannot be attributed to the drug night, because that group scored lower on every day.
